variables.title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
variables.abstract:
We introduce a new language representation model called BERT, which stands for Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers. Unlike recent language representation models, BERT is designed to pre-train deep bidirectional representations from unlabeled text by jointly conditioning on both left and right context in all layers. As a result, the pre-trained BERT model can be fine-tuned with just one additional output layer to create state-of-the-art models for a wide range of tasks, such as question answering and language inference, without substantial task-specific architecture modifications.
  BERT is conceptually simple and empirically powerful. It obtains new state-of-the-art results on eleven natural language processing tasks, including pushing the GLUE score to 80.5% (7.7% point absolute improvement), MultiNLI accuracy to 86.7% (4.6% absolute improvement), SQuAD v1.1 question answering Test F1 to 93.2 (1.5 point absolute improvement) and SQuAD v2.0 Test F1 to 83.1 (5.1 point absolute improvement).
variables.sections_xml:
<sections>
<section name="Introduction">Existing pre-trained language models are constrained by unidirectionality, which hinders downstream task performance. BERT overcomes this by using masked language modeling and next-sentence prediction to enable deep bidirectional representations, setting new state-of-the-art results across eleven NLP benchmarks.</section>
<section name="Related Work">Contextualizes BERT within existing pre-training paradigms, distinguishing between feature-based models like ELMo and fine-tuning approaches like OpenAI GPT. It establishes that prior methods rely on unidirectional models or shallow concatenation, highlighting the gap BERT's deeply bidirectional approach fills.</section>
<section name="BERT">BERT establishes a unified two-step framework of pre-training and fine-tuning using a bidirectional Transformer encoder. It also details the model configurations (Base and Large) and a flexible input representation that packs single or paired sentences using token, segment, and position embeddings.</section>
<section name="Experiments">Fine-tuning BERT with minimal task-specific parameters establishes new state-of-the-art results across diverse NLP benchmarks, including GLUE and SQuAD. Both model variants substantially outperform prior systems like OpenAI GPT, with BERT-Large delivering the largest gains even on small datasets.</section>
<section name="Ablation Studies">This section proves that both deep bidirectionality and next-sentence prediction are essential to BERT's performance, as removing either component causes notable accuracy drops across tasks. It also shows that scaling up model size consistently leads to substantial improvements on downstream tasks.</section>
<section name="Conclusion">Unsupervised pre-training is critical for language understanding, and BERT's core breakthrough is extending this approach to deep bidirectional models that generalize across a broad spectrum of NLP tasks.</section>
<section name="Additional Details for BERT">This section contrasts BERT's architecture with OpenAI GPT and ELMo, providing concrete implementation details and examples for the masking strategy and next sentence prediction tasks.</section>
<section name="Detailed Experimental Setup">Defines the individual tasks and data characteristics that comprise the GLUE benchmark used to evaluate the model, along with specific evaluation choices such as excluding WNLI. Presenters can use this to provide context on the benchmark's breadth across inference, sentiment, and paraphrase tasks.</section>
<section name="Additional Ablation Studies">This section shows that extensive pre-training steps continuously improve downstream accuracy and validates that BERT's mixed 80/10/10 masking strategy effectively mitigates pre-train and fine-tune mismatch.</section>
</sections>

variables.title: One Step Diffusion via Shortcut Models
variables.abstract: Diffusion models and flow-matching models have enabled generating diverse and realistic images by learning to transfer noise to data. However, sampling from these models involves iterative denoising over many neural network passes, making generation slow and expensive. Previous approaches for speeding up sampling require complex training regimes, such as multiple training phases, multiple networks, or fragile scheduling. We introduce shortcut models, a family of generative models that use a single network and training phase to produce high-quality samples in a single or multiple sampling steps. Shortcut models condition the network not only on the current noise level but also on the desired step size, allowing the model to skip ahead in the generation process. Across a wide range of sampling step budgets, shortcut models consistently produce higher quality samples than previous approaches, such as consistency models and reflow. Compared to distillation, shortcut models reduce complexity to a single network and training phase and additionally allow varying step budgets at inference time.
variables.sections_xml:
<sections>
<section name="Introduction">Shortcut models enable high-quality generation across any inference budget—including a single step—by conditioning directly on the desired step size during a single training run. This eliminates the need for complex multi-stage distillation or delicate scheduling while matching standard diffusion quality.</section>
<section name="Background">Flow-matching trains a model to predict the average velocity from noise to data, which works well in continuous time but inherently fails in few-step or single-step generation because the initial prediction points toward the dataset mean rather than a specific mode.</section>
<section name="Shortcut Models for Few Step Generation">Shortcut models enable flexible, few-step generation by conditioning on both timestep and step size to account for trajectory curvature. They are trained efficiently without costly ODE simulation by combining flow-matching with a self-consistency objective where a single large step equals two consecutive half-steps.</section>
<section name="Related Work">This section contrasts shortcut models against diffusion distillation and consistency models, showing they train end-to-end without multi-phase pipelines. Compared to consistency models, shortcut models eliminate discretization bias by sampling from the learned ODE, require exponentially fewer bootstrap steps, and bypass complex training tricks.</section>
<section name="Experiments">This section evaluates shortcut models against major two-stage and end-to-end diffusion baselines using a unified DiT-B setup. It demonstrates that the approach achieves competitive few- and one-step generation quality without sacrificing many-step performance, while maintaining strong scalability and robustness.</section>
<section name="Discussion">Shortcut models enable simple, single-phase training for fast one-step and few-step diffusion generation without complex distillation pipelines. While stable and versatile across domains like images and robotics, open challenges remain in closing the quality gap between one-step and multi-step sampling.</section>
<section name="Acknowledgements">Credits funding from the National Science Foundation, clarifies institutional disclaimers, and acknowledges Google TPU Research Cloud for compute support.</section>
<section name="Appendix">Provides visual generation samples across varying step budgets and demonstrates that scaling the Shortcut Model to larger architectures yields competitive image quality against state-of-the-art diffusion and adversarial baselines.</section>
<section name="Training Details">Provides experimental configurations across datasets and standardizes baseline implementations to ensure fair, equal-compute comparisons.</section>
</sections>

sections: Shortcut Models for Few Step Generation

variables.title: Mixture-of-Experts with Expert Choice Routing
variables.abstract: Sparsely-activated Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models allow the number of parameters to greatly increase while keeping the amount of computation for a given token or a given sample unchanged. However, a poor expert routing strategy (e.g. one resulting in load imbalance) can cause certain experts to be under-trained, leading to an expert being under or over-specialized. Prior work allocates a fixed number of experts to each token using a top-k function regardless of the relative importance of different tokens. To address this, we propose a heterogeneous mixture-of-experts employing an expert choice method. Instead of letting tokens select the top-k experts, we have experts selecting the top-k tokens. As a result, each token can be routed to a variable number of experts and each expert can have a fixed bucket size. We systematically study pre-training speedups using the same computational resources of the Switch Transformer top-1 and GShard top-2 gating of prior work and find that our method improves training convergence time by more than 2x. For the same computational cost, our method demonstrates higher performance in fine-tuning 11 selected tasks in the GLUE and SuperGLUE benchmarks. For a smaller activation cost, our method outperforms the T5 dense model in 7 out of the 11 tasks.
variables.sections_xml:
<sections>
<section name="Introduction">This section highlights the inefficiency and load imbalance of traditional token-choice routing in Mixture-of-Experts models. It introduces a novel expert-choice method where experts select tokens, ensuring perfect load balancing and significantly faster training convergence.</section>
<section name="Related Work">This section reviews existing approaches to model scaling and Mixture of Experts, noting that prior methods struggle with load balancing and rely on fragile auxiliary losses. It positions the proposed approach as a more robust, learned alternative that supports heterogeneous experts and improves downstream fine-tuning.</section>
<section name="Method">This section outlines the flaws of traditional token-choice routing, such as load imbalance and rigid compute allocation, and introduces the proposed expert-choice method. By having experts select top tokens instead of the reverse, this approach guarantees perfect load balancing and allows flexible compute scaling based on token complexity.</section>
<section name="Experiments">This section details the experimental setup, including the 1.6-trillion token dataset and GLUE/SuperGLUE evaluation benchmarks. It demonstrates that the proposed Expert Choice routing achieves over 2x faster training convergence and higher downstream task accuracy compared to baseline methods.</section>
<section name="Conclusion">This section summarizes the newly proposed mixture-of-experts routing method, showing how it solves load imbalance and allows variable expert selection. It highlights the model's 2x training efficiency improvement and strong benchmark results compared to existing baselines.</section>
<section name="Limitations">This section highlights the model's current constraints, specifically its incompatibility with auto-regressive text generation, poor handling of small inference batch sizes, and the high memory footprint typical of MoE architectures. It also outlines potential engineering workarounds and future improvements to address these issues.</section>
<section name="Checklist">This section provides the standard conference checklist confirming reproducibility, ethical compliance, and data usage details. It contains no core research content and can typically be skipped for presentation planning.</section>
</sections>

variables.title: Scaling Up Visual and Vision-Language Representation Learning With Noisy Text Supervision
variables.abstract: Pre-trained representations are becoming crucial for many NLP and perception tasks. While representation learning in NLP has transitioned to training on raw text without human annotations, visual and vision-language representations still rely heavily on curated training datasets that are expensive or require expert knowledge. For vision applications, representations are mostly learned using datasets with explicit class labels such as ImageNet or OpenImages. For vision-language, popular datasets like Conceptual Captions, MSCOCO, or CLIP all involve a non-trivial data collection (and cleaning) process. This costly curation process limits the size of datasets and hence hinders the scaling of trained models. In this paper, we leverage a noisy dataset of over one billion image alt-text pairs, obtained without expensive filtering or post-processing steps in the Conceptual Captions dataset. A simple dual-encoder architecture learns to align visual and language representations of the image and text pairs using a contrastive loss. We show that the scale of our corpus can make up for its noise and leads to state-of-the-art representations even with such a simple learning scheme. Our visual representation achieves strong performance when transferred to classification tasks such as ImageNet and VTAB. The aligned visual and language representations enables zero-shot image classification and also set new state-of-the-art results on Flickr30K and MSCOCO image-text retrieval benchmarks, even when compared with more sophisticated cross-attention models. The representations also enable cross-modality search with complex text and text + image queries.
variables.sections_xml:
<sections>
<section name="Introduction">ALIGN overcomes the data bottlenecks of curated vision-language datasets by training a simple dual-encoder model on over one billion minimally filtered, noisy image-text pairs. This massive scale reliably outperforms existing methods, achieving state-of-the-art results in cross-modal retrieval and zero-shot classification.</section>
<section name="Related Work">Existing vision-language models typically rely on slow cross-attention architectures or heavily curated datasets like CLIP's vocabulary-filtered pairs. ALIGN shows that a simpler, fast dual-encoder trained directly on raw, uncurated web text can outperform complex models while remaining practical for real-world retrieval.</section>
<section name="A Large-Scale Noisy Image-Text Dataset">By relaxing aggressive curation and applying only minimal frequency-based filters, the authors scale up training data to 1.8 billion noisy image-text pairs from raw web alt-text.</section>
<section name="Pre-training and Task Transfer">ALIGN trains dual image-text encoders from scratch using a normalized softmax contrastive loss across large cross-core batches. The resulting representations are evaluated across cross-modal retrieval, semantic similarity, zero-shot ImageNet benchmarks, and fine-grained visual classification tasks.</section>
<section name="Experiments and Results">Details the large-scale training setup and demonstrates that ALIGN achieves state-of-the-art cross-modal retrieval results across standard benchmarks in both zero-shot and fine-tuned settings.</section>
<section name="Ablation Study">Model performance scales steadily with larger image and text backbones, confirming that maximum capacity yields the best representations. Additionally, larger embedding dimensions, full in-batch negatives, and a learnable softmax temperature are essential design choices.</section>
<section name="Analysis of Learned Embeddings">ALIGN's shared embedding space demonstrates strong cross-modal compositionality and generalization to novel, complex concepts. This enables precise text-to-image retrieval and multimodal arithmetic queries, allowing users to modify or remove image attributes via vector addition and subtraction.</section>
<section name="Multilingual ALIGN Model">By lifting language constraints to train on 1.8 billion multilingual web pairs, ALIGN scales seamlessly across 100+ languages. In zero-shot cross-lingual retrieval, it dramatically outperforms existing zero-shot baselines and rivals fully fine-tuned models.</section>
<section name="Conclusion">ALIGN demonstrates that training a simple dual-encoder on massive, minimally filtered noisy image-text pairs can match or exceed state-of-the-art models on both vision-language and vision-only benchmarks without expensive data curation.</section>
<section name="Social Impacts and Future Work">Deploying models trained on raw web data requires rigorous auditing and data balancing to prevent reinforcing stereotypes, demographic biases, and harmful associations. Strict safeguards are also necessary to prohibit malicious applications such as surveillance.</section>
<section name="Remove Near-Duplicate Test Images from Training Data">To prevent benchmark contamination, the authors use a specialized embedding model and cluster-based bucketing to detect and remove training images that closely match downstream test images based on a strict cosine similarity threshold.</section>
<section name="Evaluation on SimLex-999">ALIGN word embeddings perform competitively on SimLex-999 and outperform text-only GloVe on concrete nouns and hard word pairs. This demonstrates that visual co-training helps models distinguish genuine semantic similarity from mere relatedness.</section>
</sections>

sections: Remove Near-Duplicate Test Images from Training Data

variables.title: Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces
variables.abstract: Foundation models, now powering most of the exciting applications in deep learning, are almost universally based on the Transformer architecture and its core attention module. Many subquadratic-time architectures such as linear attention, gated convolution and recurrent models, and structured state space models (SSMs) have been developed to address Transformers' computational inefficiency on long sequences, but they have not performed as well as attention on important modalities such as language. We identify that a key weakness of such models is their inability to perform content-based reasoning, and make several improvements. First, simply letting the SSM parameters be functions of the input addresses their weakness with discrete modalities, allowing the model to selectively propagate or forget information along the sequence length dimension depending on the current token. Second, even though this change prevents the use of efficient convolutions, we design a hardware-aware parallel algorithm in recurrent mode. We integrate these selective SSMs into a simplified end-to-end neural network architecture without attention or even MLP blocks (Mamba). Mamba enjoys fast inference (5$\times$ higher throughput than Transformers) and linear scaling in sequence length, and its performance improves on real data up to million-length sequences. As a general sequence model backbone, Mamba achieves state-of-the-art performance across several modalities such as language, audio, and genomics. On language modeling, our Mamba-3B model outperforms Transformers of the same size and matches Transformers twice its size, both in pretraining and downstream evaluation.
variables.sections_xml:
<sections>
<section name="Introduction">While Transformers dominate sequence modeling despite quadratic scaling and SSMs offer linear efficiency but struggle on dense modalities like text, the authors introduce selective state space models with a hardware-aware algorithm to achieve Transformer-level capability at linear speed.</section>
<section name="State Space Models">Establishes how standard State Space Models discretize continuous systems into dual representations: parallel convolutions for training and linear recurrences for fast inference. It highlights Linear Time Invariance (LTI) as the foundational mechanism that enables this duality but keeps dynamics constant over time.</section>
<section name="Selective State Space Models">Sequence modeling fundamentally requires compressing context into a compact state, which traditional time-invariant models fail at because their static dynamics cannot selectively filter information based on content. Introducing input-dependent selectivity allows models to retain only relevant information, bridging the gap between recurrent efficiency and attention-level expressiveness.</section>
<section name="Empirical Evaluation">Establishes the experimental roadmap across multiple domains and demonstrates on synthetic tasks that Mamba's selection mechanism enables content-dependent recall and in-context learning where prior SSMs fail.</section>
<section name="Discussion">Highlights Mamba's trade-offs and open challenges, noting that gains on discrete data may compromise continuous-signal performance and that scaling to massive models while matching Transformer downstream affordances remains untested.</section>
<section name="Conclusion">Mamba demonstrates that adding a linear-scaling selection mechanism to state space models can match or outperform Transformers across diverse domains. This establishes selective SSMs as a promising general-purpose backbone, especially for long-sequence modalities like genomics, audio, and video.</section>
<section name="Discussion: Selection Mechanism">This section clarifies how selection differs from vaguely defined concepts like gating and hypernetworks, defining it specifically as a mechanism to control information flow along the sequence dimension akin to traditional RNN gating.</section>
<section name="Related Work">This section surveys prior structured state space models and architectures, emphasizing that earlier approaches were strictly linear time-invariant. It highlights how the proposed model departs from predecessors by introducing an input-dependent selection mechanism combined with a hardware-aware scan.</section>
<section name="Mechanics of Selective SSMs">Proves mathematically that discretizing a continuous-time selective SSM directly yields classical input-dependent gating. This establishes a formal connection showing that standard recurrent gating is a special case of selective state space models.</section>
<section name="Hardware-aware Algorithm For Selective SSMs">To overcome GPU memory-bandwidth bottlenecks caused by input-dependent states, the authors design a hardware-aware algorithm using kernel fusion and activation recomputation in fast SRAM. This eliminates slow HBM reads/writes, making selective SSMs up to 40x faster and matching the memory footprint of FlashAttention.</section>
<section name="Full Experiments">Provides comprehensive empirical evaluations across controlled synthetic benchmarks and real-world genomic DNA sequence modeling tasks.</section>
<section name="Experimental Details and Additional Results">Provides technical training setups and highlights that Mamba uniquely achieves perfect length generalization up to one million tokens on synthetic induction heads, whereas attention models run out of memory and competing sub-quadratic baselines degrade.</section>
</sections>

variables.title: Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units
variables.abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) models typically operate with a fixed vocabulary, but translation is an open-vocabulary problem. Previous work addresses the translation of out-of-vocabulary words by backing off to a dictionary. In this paper, we introduce a simpler and more effective approach, making the NMT model capable of open-vocabulary translation by encoding rare and unknown words as sequences of subword units. This is based on the intuition that various word classes are translatable via smaller units than words, for instance names (via character copying or transliteration), compounds (via compositional translation), and cognates and loanwords (via phonological and morphological transformations). We discuss the suitability of different word segmentation techniques, including simple character n-gram models and a segmentation based on the byte pair encoding compression algorithm, and empirically show that subword models improve over a back-off dictionary baseline for the WMT 15 translation tasks English-German and English-Russian by 1.1 and 1.3 BLEU, respectively.
variables.sections_xml:
<sections>
<section name="Introduction">Standard neural machine translation fails on rare and unseen words due to fixed vocabularies and ineffective dictionary back-offs. To solve this, the paper introduces Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) for subword segmentation, enabling effective open-vocabulary translation directly within the neural model.</section>
<section name="Neural Machine Translation">Summarizes the standard Bahdanau attentional encoder-decoder architecture used for the experiments, emphasizing that the paper's proposed method is architecture-agnostic.</section>
<section name="Subword Translation">Most rare words—such as named entities, cognates, and compounds—have transparent meanings that can be derived from smaller subword units. Segmenting words into these subwords allows neural translation models to learn and generalize transparent translations to completely unseen vocabulary.</section>
<section name="Evaluation">This section outlines the experimental setup across English-to-German and English-to-Russian tasks, detailing the metrics and benchmarks used to test whether subword units improve the translation of rare and unseen words.</section>
<section name="Analysis">Subword models outperform large-vocabulary and dictionary back-off baselines on rare and out-of-vocabulary words by productively generating compounds and transliterations instead of merely copying source tokens. Furthermore, using a smaller vocabulary of subword units mitigates data sparsity, stabilizing translation accuracy for low-frequency words.</section>
<section name="Conclusion">Subword segmentation via BPE effectively solves open-vocabulary translation with a compact vocabulary, eliminating the need for complex back-off models. The authors conclude that subwords improve rare-word handling across language pairs and highlight future work on automatically finding optimal vocabulary sizes.</section>
</sections>

variables.title: AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data
variables.sections_xml:
<sections>
<section name="What is model collapse?">Defines model collapse as a degenerative cycle where recursively training generative models on synthetic data erodes distribution tails and eventually destroys diversity. It identifies three compounding error mechanisms driving this failure: finite sampling noise, model capacity limits, and algorithmic learning biases.</section>
<section name="Theoretical intuition">Establishes a mathematical framework showing that recursive training across generations is an absorbing Markov chain that inherently suffers from statistical sampling error. Even with ideal functional approximation, low-probability events disappear until the distribution inevitably collapses into a single-state delta function.</section>
<section name="Model collapse in language models">This section tests recursive fine-tuning on language models to demonstrate that training purely on model-generated data degrades performance, while retaining a small fraction of real data helps mitigate collapse.</section>
<section name="Discussion">Automating model-generated content causes widespread distribution shifts that threaten fairness by erasing rare events, giving early developers trained on clean human data a lasting first-mover advantage. To prevent collapse, the field urgently needs large-scale data provenance tracking or community coordination to separate human-generated text from AI content.</section>
<section name="Online content">Contains administrative metadata, data availability links, and citations, which are not suitable for slide content.</section>
<section name="Data availability">This section directs readers to external references for accessing the datasets and data-generation code used across the GMM, VAE, and LLM experiments.</section>
<section name="Code availability">All experimental code is publicly accessible to ensure reproducibility, accompanied by standard author contributions, acknowledgements, and publication disclosures.</section>
</sections>

variables.title: Action-aware Dynamic Pruning for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Manipulation
variables.abstract: Robotic manipulation with Vision-Language-Action models requires efficient inference over long-horizon multi-modal context, where attention to dense visual tokens dominates computational cost. Existing methods optimize inference speed by reducing visual redundancy within VLA models, but they overlook the varying redundancy across robotic manipulation stages. We observe that the visual token redundancy is higher in coarse manipulation phase than in fine-grained operations, and is strongly correlated with the action dynamic. Motivated by this observation, we propose \textbf{A}ction-aware \textbf{D}ynamic \textbf{P}runing (\textbf{ADP}), a multi-modal pruning framework that integrates text-driven token selection with action-aware trajectory gating. Our method introduces a gating mechanism that conditions the pruning signal on recent action trajectories, using past motion windows to adaptively adjust token retention ratios in accordance with dynamics, thereby balancing computational efficiency and perceptual precision across different manipulation stages. Extensive experiments on the LIBERO suites and diverse real-world scenarios demonstrate that our method significantly reduces FLOPs and action inference latency (\textit{e.g.} $1.35 \times$ speed up on OpenVLA-OFT) while maintaining competitive success rates (\textit{e.g.} 25.8\% improvements with OpenVLA) compared to baselines, thereby providing a simple plug-in path to efficient robot policies that advances the efficiency and performance frontier of robotic manipulation. Our project website is: \href{https://vla-adp.github.io/}{ADP.com}.
variables.sections_xml:
<sections>
<section name="Introduction">This section highlights the computational inefficiency of processing all visual tokens in robot action models and introduces Action-aware Dynamic Pruning (ADP). ADP saves compute by pruning redundant visual tokens during broad movements while preserving full visual details for delicate, precise actions.</section>
<section name="Preliminary">This section explains the baseline vision-language-action framework used by OpenVLA to translate images and text into robotic movements. It contrasts the standard autoregressive approach with an optimized parallel decoding method for faster, multi-step action generation.</section>
<section name="Related Work">This section reviews existing Vision-Language-Action models and current methods for improving their computational efficiency. It establishes the gap that prior efficiency techniques rely on static rules, missing the opportunity to leverage stage-dependent redundancies during robotic tasks.</section>
<section name="Methodology">This section outlines the Action-aware Dynamic Pruning method, which uses recent robot movements to dictate when pruning occurs. It also explains how text instructions filter out irrelevant visual data, reducing computational load while keeping focus on task-critical features.</section>
<section name="EXPERIMENTS">This section evaluates the proposed model on simulated and real-robot tasks to measure success rates, latency, and computational efficiency against various baselines. The results demonstrate that the method maintains high success rates while significantly reducing compute costs and increasing inference speed through targeted visual token pruning.</section>
<section name="Ablation Study">This section isolates the model's core components to prove that both the action-aware dynamic strategy and the text-driven pruning module are essential. The data demonstrates that removing either piece significantly reduces the model's overall success rate.</section>
<section name="Conclusion">This section concludes the paper by confirming that the VLA-ADP framework successfully speeds up inference and cuts compute costs without hurting task performance. It highlights that combining a dynamic controller with early-layer scoring provides the optimal balance between efficiency and robotic control quality.</section>
</sections>
